claims.text: High-energy mechanical alloying followed by rapid consolidation can produce a stable, fine-grained RHEA–Cu composite microstructure.
The proposed process will minimize intermetallic formation despite the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
High-energy mechanical alloying can homogenize a mixture of RHEA and Cu powders.
Spark plasma sintering or a similar rapid densification method can consolidate the mechanically alloyed RHEA–Cu powder.
An inert milling atmosphere prevents oxidation during mechanical alloying.
Controlling sintering temperature, pressure, and dwell time can minimize excessive diffusion or reaction between phases.
Mechanical alloying forces intimate mixing of Cu and refractory elements.
Mechanical alloying refines grain sizes in the RHEA–Cu powder mixture.
Mechanical alloying creates a metastable solution in the RHEA–Cu system.
Rapid bipolar pulsed heating during spark plasma sintering suppresses extended interdiffusion.
Suppressing extended interdiffusion during rapid sintering reduces intermetallic formation.
Repeated fracturing and cold welding during milling homogeneously distribute Cu and refractory elements.
A short sintering cycle limits chemical reactions in the RHEA–Cu composite.
Mechanical alloying and rapid sintering enhance phase stability in the RHEA–Cu composite.
Mechanical alloying and rapid sintering improve the mechanical properties of the RHEA–Cu composite.
Mechanical alloying and rapid sintering improve the thermal stability of the RHEA–Cu composite.
The resulting composite will be suitable for high-temperature nuclear applications.
Conventional melting or slow powder consolidation of RHEA–Cu composites causes severe elemental segregation or brittle intermetallic formation.
Milling conditions, composition, sintering temperature, pressure, and holding time determine whether adequate mixing and reaction suppression are achieved.
